resposta:
A Copa Libertadores de 2025 já foi concluída — o Flamengo conquistou o tetra ao vencer o Palmeiras na final. Os **8 times brasileiros** que se classificaram foram os seguintes:

## Times brasileiros classificados para a Libertadores 2025

| Time | Vaga conquistada | Fase inicial |
|------|------------------|--------------|
| **Botafogo** | Campeão da Libertadores 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **Flamengo** | Campeão da Copa do Brasil 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **Palmeiras** | Vice-campeão do Brasileirão 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **Fortaleza** | 4º colocado do Brasileirão 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **Internacional** | 5º colocado do Brasileirão 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **São Paulo** | 6º colocado do Brasileirão 2024 | Fase de grupos |
| **Corinthians** | 7º colocado do Brasileirão 2024 | Segunda fase (playoff) |
| **Bahia** | 8º colocado do Brasileirão 2024 | Segunda fase (playoff) |

### Como as vagas foram distribuídas
- **Botafogo**: campeão da Libertadores 2024 (vaga automática em grupo)
- **Flamengo**: vencedor da Copa do Brasil 2024 (vaga adicional além das 7 do Brasileirão)
- **Palmeiras a Bahia**: ocuparam as demais 7 vagas do Campeonato Brasileiro de 2024, de vice até 8º lugar

### Desempenho na competição
Os brasileiros tiveram um bom desempenho:
- **Palmeiras** chegou à final e ficou com o **vice-campeonato**
- **Flamengo** venceu a final e conquistou o **título**
- **São Paulo**, **Internacional** e **Botafogo** caíram nas quartas de final ou antes
- **Corinthians** e **Bahia** não avançaram além da segunda fase preliminar (o Corinthians foi eliminado pelo Barcelona de Guayaquil; o Bahia caiu para o Cerro Porteño)

O destaque brasileiro na competição foi o **Flamengo**, que teve três jogadores na Seleção da Libertadores 2025, incluindo o craque do torneio **Giorgian de Arrascaeta**.

A **[Copa Libertadores da América](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América "Copa Libertadores da América") de 2025**, oficialmente **CONMEBOL Libertadores 2025**, foi a 66.ª edição da competição de futebol realizada anualmente pela [Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") (CONMEBOL). Participaram clubes das dez associações [sul-americanas](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/América_do_Sul "América do Sul").

Em uma reedição da [final de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021"), dessa vez o [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") superou o [Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") por 1–0 no [Estádio Monumental](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") em [Lima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), Peru, para conquistar seu quarto título na competição, além de se tornar o primeiro clube brasileiro a atingir esse feito.[[2]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-2)

Como campeão, representou a CONMEBOL na [Copa Intercontinental de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Intercontinental_da_FIFA_de_2025 "Copa Intercontinental da FIFA de 2025"). No ano seguinte, enfrentará o [Lanús](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Lanús "Club Atlético Lanús"), campeão da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2025 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2025"), na [Recopa Sul-Americana de 2026](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recopa_Sul-Americana_de_2026 "Recopa Sul-Americana de 2026"), assim como se classificou automaticamente para a fase de grupos da [Copa Libertadores da América de 2026](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2026 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2026") e para a segunda edição do quadrienal [Mundial de Clubes FIFA](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA "Mundial de Clubes FIFA"), em [2029](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA_de_2029 "Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2029").[[3]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-3)

- Campeão da Copa Libertadores da América de 2024
- Campeão da Copa Sul-Americana de 2024
- Brasil: 7 vagas
- Argentina: 6 vagas

- **Fase de grupos: 28 equipes**

  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 1 e 2 de todas as outras associações

  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 6 e 7 do Brasil
  - Equipe que qualificou para a vaga 6 da Argentina
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 3 e 4 do Chile e Colômbia
  - Equipes qualificadas para a vaga 3 de todas as outras associações.
- **Primeira fase: 6 equipes**
  - Equipes que se qualificaram para a vaga 4 da Bolívia, Equador, Paraguai, Peru, Uruguai e Venezuela

Em contrato firmado com a CONMEBOL para o Brasil, a [TV Globo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Globo "TV Globo") transmitiu a competição em [sinal aberto](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinal_aberto "Sinal aberto"). As exibições seguiram com [ESPN](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_(Brasil) "ESPN (Brasil)") na [TV fechada](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_fechada "TV fechada") e com [Disney+](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney+ "Disney+") e [Paramount+](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") no *[streaming](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming "Streaming")*.[[21]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-23)

## Fases preliminares

Ver artigo principal: [Fases preliminares da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fases_preliminares_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2025 "Fases preliminares da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025")

As etapas de qualificação estão estruturadas da seguinte forma:

- **Primeira fase** (6 equipes): os três vencedores da primeira fase avançam para a segunda fase para se juntarem às 13 equipes que recebem folga para a segunda fase
- **Segunda fase** (16 equipes): os oito vencedores da segunda fase avançam para a terceira fase
- **Terceira fase** (8 equipes): os quatro vencedores da terceira fase avançam para a fase de grupos para se juntarem aos 28 participantes diretos. As quatro equipes eliminadas na terceira fase entram na fase de grupos da Copa Sul-Americana de 2025

A chave foi decidida com base no sorteio da primeira fase e do sorteio da segunda fase, que foi realizado em 19 de dezembro de 2024.[[18]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sorteio-18)[[19]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-conmebollibertadores_sorteio-19)

## Fase de grupos

Ver artigo principal: [Fase de grupos da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fase_de_grupos_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2025 "Fase de grupos da Copa Libertadores da América de 2025")

Os vencedores e os segundos classificados de cada grupo avançam para as oitavas de final, enquanto os terceiros colocados serão transferidos para os *play-offs* da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2025 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2025").[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-regulam-24)

Nessa fase, cada grupo é disputado em turno e returno, todos contra todos. As equipes são classificadas de acordo com os seguintes critérios:[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-regulam-24)

1. Pontos (três pontos por vitória, um ponto por empate e nenhum ponto por derrota)
2. Saldo de gols;
3. Gols marcados;
4. Gols marcados fora de casa;
5. [Ranking CONMEBOL](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_CONMEBOL "Ranking CONMEBOL").

### Equipes classificadas

Após a conclusão da fase de grupos, um sorteio definiu o chaveamento das equipes classificadas a partir das oitavas de final até a final. O sorteio aconteceu na sede da CONMEBOL, em Luque, no Paraguai, em 2 de junho.[[17]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sorteio_fase_final-17) As 16 equipes foram sorteadas em oito confrontos de oitavas de final (A–H) entre um vencedor de grupo (alocados no pote 1) e um segundo colocado de grupo (alocados no pote 2), com os vencedores dos grupos realizando o jogo de volta como mandante. Equipes da mesma federação ou do mesmo grupo poderiam ser sorteadas para a mesma eliminatória.

## Final

### Escolha da sede

Em 13 de dezembro de 2024, a [Confederação Brasileira de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Brasileira_de_Futebol "Confederação Brasileira de Futebol") (CBF) formalizou a candidatura do [Estádio Nacional de Brasília Mané Garrincha](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Nacional_de_Brasília_Mané_Garrincha "Estádio Nacional de Brasília Mané Garrincha"), em [Brasília](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasília "Brasília"), capital do Brasil, como sede para a final da Copa Libertadores de 2025 — com capacidade para 70 mil pessoas, recebeu partidas da [Copa das Confederações de 2013](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_das_Confederações_FIFA_de_2013 "Copa das Confederações FIFA de 2013"), [Copa do Mundo de 2014](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_do_Mundo_FIFA_de_2014 "Copa do Mundo FIFA de 2014"), [Jogos Olímpicos do Rio 2016](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futebol_nos_Jogos_Olímpicos_de_Verão_de_2016 "Futebol nos Jogos Olímpicos de Verão de 2016") e [Copa América de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_América_de_2021 "Copa América de 2021"). Caso a entidade escolhesse o estádio, seria a terceira final nos últimos cinco anos em estádio brasileiros — anteriormente as decisões de [2020](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2020 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2020") (realizada em 2021) e [2023](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2023 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2023") aconteceram no [Estádio do Maracanã](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Jornalista_Mário_Filho "Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho"), [Rio de Janeiro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro").[[27]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-uol_sede_brasilia-30)

Além da candidatura de Brasília, as cidades de [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu"), no Uruguai, e [Lima](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), no Peru, também disputaram o direito de sediar a final com os estádios [Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario") (capacidade de 43 mil torcedores) e [Monumental "U"](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") (capacidade de 80 mil torcedores), respectivamente. O Monumental de Lima foi sede da [primeira final única](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2019 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2019") da história da Copa Libertadores, em 2019, entre [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") e [River Plate](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_River_Plate "Club Atlético River Plate").[[28]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-31)

Em 28 de abril de 2025, a CONMEBOL anunciou Lima, no Peru, como sede da final, mas ainda sem definir o estádio onde a partida seria realizada. Essa definição deve aconteceu em função dos possíveis finalistas, evitando lugares vazios — como aconteceu em algumas finais não só da Libertadores, como da Sul-Americana.[[29]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-32)[[30]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-33) Em 11 de agosto, o [Estádio Monumental "U"](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Monumental_"U" "Estádio Monumental "U"") foi anunciado como local da partida final.[[31]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2025#cite_note-34)

# [2410.12049] Sabiá-3 Technical Report

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.12049) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4)
> Abstract:This report presents Sabiá-3, our new flagship language model, and Sabiazinho-3, a more cost-effective sibling. The models were trained on a large brazilian-centric corpus. Evaluations across diverse professional and academic benchmarks show a strong performance on Portuguese and Brazil-related tasks. Sabiá-3 shows large improvements in comparison to our previous best of model, Sabia-2 Medium, especially in reasoning-intensive tasks. Notably, Sabiá-3's average performance matches frontier LLMs, while it is offered at a three to four times lower cost per token, reinforcing the benefits of domain specialization.

1

Introduction

This technical report presents the details of the development and evaluation of  
the Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 models. We trained them on a large corpus of doc-

uments written in Portuguese, with a special focus on Brazil-related resources.  
Through training, models were exposed to information relevant to Brazilian cul-  
ture, history, and context. The main objective was to have a specialized model  
that is aware of the linguistic nuances, societal norms, and regional variations  
unique to the country. Throughout this report, we show that this specialization  
allows the models to perform better in knowledge-intensive tasks.

We applied an approach of continual learning by leveraging a “generalist”

model that already acquired some level of language understanding and reasoning  
abilities, and then further trained it on our corpus of high-quality data relevant  
to the Brazilian context. The development consisted of two main phases: (1) the  
pre-training phase, in which we further train a pre-trained model on specialized  
data following a self-supervised learning strategy optimizing for the next token  
prediction objective, and (2) the post-training phase where the model is tuned  
to follow instructions and align to human preferences.

Instruction-Following Capabilities

One relevant benchmark to assess LLM abilities to follow instructions is the  
IFEval [\[20\]. ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#16)IFEval consists of approximately 500 prompts including instruc-  
tions that are veriafiable programmatically such as “write in more than 400  
words”. It uses two main metrics: strict and loose. In the strict metric, the  
model’s response is checked against a set of verifiable instructions to determine  
if it followed all of them. If so, the model receives a point. If any part of the  
instruction is not followed exactly as specified, the response is deemed incorrect  
and the model does not receive a point. The loose metric is more lenient as  
it considers variations and common transformations that might occur in the  
model’s response. For example, if an instruction requires a specific phrase to be  
included at the end of an email, but the model includes that phrase with addi-  
tional text formatting like bold or italics, the loose metric might still consider

the instruction to be followed, whereas the strict metric would not.

Since this benchmark’s prompts and target answers are in English, we do

not expect our Portuguese-specialized model to yield significant improvements  
in this scenario. Instead, this benchmark primarily serves to assess how well  
our model can follow instructions in comparison to state-of-the-art LLMs.

2.5

Function Calling Capabilities

The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [\[17\] ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#15)is a benchmark for  
evaluating the LLM’s capabilities in executing function calls and using tools  
effectively. The benchmark is updated periodically, and comprises three distinct  
subsets:

1\. Non-live: An expert-curated collection of question-function-answer pairs,

encompassing multiple languages and complex use cases, designed to chal-  
lenge the models’ ability to understand and apply functions accurately.  
The examples are categorized into Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) analysis,  
measuring whether the function names, arguments, and parameter types  
match the expected response; and executable verification (Exec), which  
executes the function and verifies whether the output is correct.

2\. Live: User-contributed examples that reflect real-world applications, en-

suring that the models are tested against scenarios that mirror everyday  
tasks.

9

3\. Multi turn: Multi-turn and multi-step function calling tasks that simulate

agentic behaviors, requiring models to plan execution strategies, request  
information, and manage a sequence of function invocations to complete  
a task.

The benchmark also includes two categories to measure hallucinations: irrel-

evance detection, when none of the provided functions is relevant to the query  
and should not be invoked; and relevance, when at least one of the functions  
should be invoked.

2.6

Agentic Performance

Recent advancements in the ability of LLMs on instruction-following, function  
calling, and reason in long contexts have enabled the development of LLM-  
based agents. These agents can automatically execute complex tasks, such as  
developing code [\[18, ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#16)[4\], ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#13)managing everyday user tasks on operating systems  
[\[11, 12\], ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#14)and orchestrating robots [\[3\].](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#13)

To evaluate an LLM in agentic tasks, it is necessary to integrate it with a

framework with modules for memory, action, and reasoning. This setup allows  
the LLM to interact with responsive environments through tools using natu-  
ral language. To this end, we use AgentBench [\[10\], ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#14)a framework designed to  
evaluate the agentic capabilities of LLMs across eight distinct environments.  
It tests the model’s performance in multi-turn open-ended generation scenarios  
involving coding, gaming, and web.

Here are the eight environments where the agent LLM performs tasks in

AgentBench:

• Operating System (OS): Interacts with a real Ubuntu terminal, executing

bash scripts to retrieve information about the virtual OS.

• Database (DB): Runs SQL queries on a database to answer high-level

questions about multiple tables.

10

 link to page 11 link to page 14 

• Knowledge Graph (KG): Navigates a knowledge graph with 45 million

entities and 3 billion facts to extract high-level insights about relationships  
between entities.

• Web Shopping (WS): Navigates an online shopping environment to make

purchases from a web page.

• Web Browsing (WB): Browses web pages across various domains to extract

information or perform high-level actions.

• Digital Card Game (DCG): Plays a game against a rule-based agent, an-

alyzing cards with different abilities to defeat the opponent.

• Lateral Thinking Puzzle (LTP): Solves riddles by asking questions where

another agent LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) can only respond with “yes”, “no”,  
or “irrelevant”.

• House-Holding (HH): Explores a virtual house, interacting with objects

and performing high-level tasks.

Table [5 ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#11)presents the results, using the same metrics defined in the Agent-

Bench paper [\[10\]. ](1793420826925-8da54a8d-f015-4a7f-b15b-81bf2cad0c02-file27323.html#14)Each environment metric ranges from 0 to 100, with higher  
scores indicating better performance.

We report the Overall Average (OA)

across all environments as our primary metric. Due to the variation in mean  
scores across different environments, OA is the weighted average of tasks scores,

3

Conclusion

We introduced Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3, a family of language models focused on

Brazil-related content. They improve upon our earlier Sabi´

a-2 models, especially

in handling long texts, reasoning, and coding. Despite rivaling state-of-the-art  
proprietary and open-source models on knowledge-intensive tasks while having a  
lower per token cost, Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 still have room for improvement

in multi-step tasks and following instructions accurately, both of which we plan  
to address in future work.

# Sabiá-3 Technical Report

Thales Sales Almeida Affiliation: Rodrigo Nogueira and Ramon Pires Thiago Laitz Affiliation: Maritaca AI

###### Abstract

This report presents Sabiá-3, our new flagship language model, and Sabiazinho-3, a more cost-effective sibling. The models were trained on a large brazilian-centric corpus. Evaluations across diverse professional and academic benchmarks show a strong performance on Portuguese and Brazil-related tasks.
Sabiá-3 shows large improvements in comparison to our previous best of model, Sabia-2 Medium, especially in reasoning-intensive tasks.
Notably, Sabiá-3’s average performance matches frontier LLMs, while it is offered at a three to four times lower cost per token, reinforcing the benefits of domain specialization.

## 1 Introduction

This technical report presents the details of the development and evaluation of the Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 models. We trained them on a large corpus of documents written in Portuguese, with a special focus on Brazil-related resources. Through training, models were exposed to information relevant to Brazilian culture, history, and context. The main objective was to have a specialized model that is aware of the linguistic nuances, societal norms, and regional variations unique to the country. Throughout this report, we show that this specialization allows the models to perform better in knowledge-intensive tasks.

We applied an approach of continual learning by leveraging a “generalist” model that already acquired some level of language understanding and reasoning abilities, and then further trained it on our corpus of high-quality data relevant to the Brazilian context. The development consisted of two main phases: (1) the pre-training phase, in which we further train a pre-trained model on specialized data following a self-supervised learning strategy optimizing for the next token prediction objective, and (2) the post-training phase where the model is tuned to follow instructions and align to human preferences.

Compared to our previous release, Sabiá-2 [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib5 "")], we have collected a significantly larger volume of data for pre-training. In addition to the scale, we also improved the quality of our pre-training data by using a mixture of heuristic and model-based methods to filter out low-quality data.

Considering the challenges of training large scale models, we used TPU v5 accelerators with Jax [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib7 "")] to perform distributed training. We combined both data and model parallelism to achieve high training throughput and to ensure efficient utilization of TPU hardware.

After pre-training, we employed a mix of human-annotated and synthetically generated data to teach our base model to follow instructions [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib1 ""), [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib2 ""), [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib15 ""), [16](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib16 ""), [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib13 ""), [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib8 "")]. The instruction tuning data is composed of both human-annotated prompts and synthetically generated instructions targeting specific capabilities. In addition, we also include synthetic examples to induct self-awareness abilities in the model [[6](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib6 "")].

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/price_vs_performance_en.png)Figure 1: Price in USD per million tokens, considering an equal proportion of input and output tokens, versus performance on 70 Brazilian exams (in Portuguese). The dashed curve represents a Pareto frontier for general-purpose LLMs such as Llama 3.1 and GPT-4o, which Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 surpass due to their domain specialization.

## 2 Evaluation

In this section, we compare Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 with proprietary and open-source LLMs, listed in Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report"), on various benchmarks.

Table 1: Overview of the models evaluated in this work, with pricing information as of October 14, 2024. The API pricing for Llama 3.1 is from together.ai.

### 2.1 Multiple-choice Exams

We have developed a benchmark suite to evaluate the Sabiá-3 performance on 93 academic exams, including entry-level, undergraduate, and professional certification exams. Our focus is on multiple-choice questions from various Brazilian educational assessments, particularly those administered after the middle of 2023 to mitigate the risk of data contamination. However, ENADE is an exception, including spans of 2022 and 2023 to cover a wide range of disciplines.

For more details about the datasets, we recommend the readers to the Sabiá-2 technical report [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib5 "")].
In addition to the 8 benchmarks introduced in [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib5 "")], we now incorporated five new multiple-choice benchmarks:

- •     ENAM: The examination aims to qualify law graduates interested in participating in magistracy selection processes promoted by federal regional courts, labor courts, military courts, and courts of the states and the Federal District and territories. The benchmark covers the first edition of the exam, administered on April 14, 2024, and its subsequent re-application one month later with a different set of questions. There are 160 questions in total.

- •
      CPNU: First edition of the Concurso Público Nacional Unificado (Unified National Public Competition), administered by the Ministry of Management and Innovation in Public Services on August 18, 2024 for filling permanent public positions. The benchmark includes eight exams with a total of 370 questions, covering the following thematic areas:

  1. 1.         Infrastructure, Exact Sciences, and Engineering;

  2. 2.         Technology, Data, and Information;

  3. 3.         Environmental, Agricultural, and Biological Sciences;

  4. 4.         Work and Public Servant Health;

  5. 5.         Education, Health, Social Development, and Human Rights;

  6. 6.         Economic Sectors and Regulation;

  7. 7.         Government Management and Public Administration; and

  8. 8.         Intermediate Level.

- •     BCB: The BCB benchmark refers to the public examination for the Central Bank of Brazil. This exam features objective questions with two possible answers: true or false. It comprises three distinct exams: basic knowledge, information technology, and economics and finance.

- •     BNDES: The BNDES benchmark is the public examination for the National Bank for Economic and Social Development. Similar to the BCB exam, it consists of objective questions with two alternatives: true or false. The benchmark includes 14 exams covering a range of subjects such as law, systems analysis, administration, architecture, economics, engineering, accounting, and psychology.

- •     CFCEQ: The CFCEQ benchmark is the technical qualification exam conducted by the Federal Accounting Council (CFC). Its purpose is to assess the knowledge and professional competence of accountants who wish to work as independent auditors in organizations regulated by the CVM, BCB, Susep, and Previc. The benchmark comprises 12 exams.

Figure [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.1 Multiple-choice Exams ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") compares the performance of Sabiá-3, Sabiá-2 Medium, and GPT-4o on the ENADE 2022 and 2023 exams. The results reveal that Sabiá-2 has a higher difficulty level in engineering and economics-related areas, as indicated by its lowest 10 accuracies. In contrast, Sabiá-3 shows a significant improvement in these challenging areas, achieving a 70% reduction in errors compared to Sabiá-2, particularly in Economics and Computer Engineering.
Moreover, Sabiá-3 demonstrates a competitive performance compared with GPT-4o, performing equally well or superior in 36 of the 54 Enade exams.
Despite these advancements, the results indicate that Sabiá-3 continues to face difficulties in certain areas, notably Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and Accounting, where it reached its lowest scores.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/Results_for_the_National_Student_Performance_Exam.png)Figure 2: Accuracies of Sabiá-3, Sabiá-2 Medium and GPT-4o on Enade 2022 and 2023 exams, ordered from low to high based on Sabiá-2 Medium performance. Sabiá-3 outperforms Sabiá-2 Medium on 76% of the exams.

Table [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2.1 Multiple-choice Exams ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") shows the scores of the models in 13 benchmarks derived from academic and professional exams applied after mid-2023. The results illustrate that Sabiá-3 has a comparable level of accuracy to GPT-4o across all 93 exams assessed. GPT-4o exhibits an advantage particularly in the Medicine benchmarks, while Sabiá-3 demonstrates a notable performance in the CPNU exams. Furthermore, Sabiá-3 surpasses Llama-3.1 405B by 2 percentage points in accuracy, performing equally or better in 62% of the exams. Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves the highest average accuracy, although it presents a higher risk of data contamination due to its training data cutoff date.

Table 2: Accuracy on academic benchmarks. The average results (last row) cover all the 93 exams applied after the middle of 2023, which is the knowledge cutoff date of Sabiá-3. Claude 3.5’s cutoff date is April of 2024, so exams released before that date might be present in its training data.

In Figure [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report"), we show the cost per token as of October 2024 in comparison to the average accuracy on the aforementioned exams. We have plotted a Pareto curve based on generalist models, i.e., the ones not specialized in the Brazilian context. Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 stay above this frontier, underscoring the cost-quality benefits that result from domain specialization.

### 2.2 Conversation Capabilities

This section presents the benchmark we use to evaluate the Sabiá-3 capabilities to engage in dialogues.

In our previous work [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib5 "")], we introduced the Brazilian Chat Evaluation (BRACEval), a benchmark inspired on MT-Bench [[19](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib19 "")] and designed to evaluate AI assistants’ performance in following instructions, engaging in multi-turn dialogues, and demonstrating knowledge specific to Brazil. BRACEval consists of 150 multi-turn questions distributed across 13 categories, including culturally relevant topics such as writing, roleplay, extraction, humanities, entity, and contradiction analysis, as well as universal categories like abstention, harmful content, reasoning, math, and coding.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/braceval.png)Figure 3: Win, tie and loss rates for Sabiá-3 against other LLMs on the BRACEval conversation benchmark according to GPT-4-turbo as a judge.

Figure [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.2 Conversation Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") compares Sabiá-3 with other LLMs on BRACEval. The judge is an LLM that is given the prompt, the answer from Sabiá-3 and another competitor model and decides which one won or a tie. We address position bias by calling the judge twice with the order of two answers swapped.

We use GPT-4-turbo (more specifically, gpt-4-1106-preview) as the judge because, in pairwise evaluations against other models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, all judges — including Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4-turbo, and GPT-4o — consistently preferred the responses from GPT-4-turbo.

Sabiá-3 shows a significant improvement over Sabiá-2 Medium, despite still having a high percentage of losses against more expensive models, such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. A noteworthy result is GPT-4o Mini, which, despite its lower per-token price, achieves a higher win rate compared to the more expensive Llama-3.1 405B in this benchmark.

Figure [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2 Conversation Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") provides a visual representation of the performance of Sabiá-3 relative to other models, across each BRACEval category. We measure the performance using the adjusted win rate, where the winner model receives one point, and in the case of a tie, both models earn 0.5 points each.
Across most categories, Sabiá-3 outperforms Sabiá-2 Medium and performs comparably to the more expensive Llama-3.1 405B model. However, it performs poorly compared to GPT-4o, particularly in coding, math, and writing. This result is consistent regardless of the judge model; using Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a judge yields similar win rates, which indicates that the result is not influenced by the use of GPT-4-turbo as the judge.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/braceval_category.png)Figure 4: Category-wise adjusted win rates of Sabiá-3 against other models on BRACEval, with 0.5 representing a tie; models that score below it are worse than Sabiá-3; above it, competitor models are superior.

### 2.3 Instruction-Following Capabilities

One relevant benchmark to assess LLM abilities to follow instructions is the IFEval [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib20 "")]. IFEval consists of approximately 500 prompts including instructions that are veriafiable programmatically such as “write in more than 400 words”. It uses two main metrics: strict and loose. In the strict metric, the model’s response is checked against a set of verifiable instructions to determine if it followed all of them. If so, the model receives a point. If any part of the instruction is not followed exactly as specified, the response is deemed incorrect and the model does not receive a point. The loose metric is more lenient as it considers variations and common transformations that might occur in the model’s response. For example, if an instruction requires a specific phrase to be included at the end of an email, but the model includes that phrase with additional text formatting like bold or italics, the loose metric might still consider the instruction to be followed, whereas the strict metric would not.

Since this benchmark’s prompts and target answers are in English, we do not expect our Portuguese-specialized model to yield significant improvements in this scenario. Instead, this benchmark primarily serves to assess how well our model can follow instructions in comparison to state-of-the-art LLMs.

The results presented in Table [3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 2.3 Instruction-Following Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") show that Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 outperform Sabiá-2 Medium in terms of instruction-following capabilities. However, it lags behind other models evaluated in this study, including cheaper options such as GPT-4o Mini and Llama-3.1 8B.

Table 3: Results on the IFeval benchmark.

### 2.4 Long Context Capabilities

Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 can process up to 32,000 tokens in a sequence. Here we evaluate how well the model uses this capacity through the Needle-in-the-Haystack (NIAH) benchmark [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib9 "")], which measures the model’s ability to find answers within a long, unrelated context. The test involves inserting a small piece of text within a larger context ranging from 1,000 to 32,000 tokens, at various depths from 0% to 100%. Since we are focusing on evaluating the performance of an LLM on Portuguese tasks, we adapt this benchmark using the book Dom Casmurro11 1 https://machadodeassis.net/texto/dom-casmurro/11503 as the context. In a random spot within the text, we insert as a needle a sentence that says “O número mágico de Campinas é {random_number}.” (“The magic number of Campinas is {random_number}.”), replacing {random_number} with a 6-digit number. Then, we provide this modified context along with the question “Qual o número mágico de Campinas?” (“What is the magic number of Campinas?”) to the model. Using regular expression, we check whether the model correctly outputs the random number as the answer.

As depicted in Figures [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 2.4 Long Context Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") and [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 2.4 Long Context Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report"), Sabiá-3 exhibited a perfect recall in our Portuguese version of the NIAH benchmark and Sabiazinho-3 reached a recall of 99.48%, consistently locating relevant information within long contexts. We acknowledge, however, that the task, due to its simplicity, may not fully capture the long-context capabilities of language models. Therefore, for a better measure of long-range comprehension skills, we need Portuguese versions of more challenging benchmarks, such as the QuALITY benchmark [[14](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib14 "")], which tests a model’s ability to answer questions about books.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/needleinhaystack_sabia-3.png)Figure 5: Performance of the Sabiá-3 model in the Portuguese-adapted Needle-in-the-Haystack (NIAH) benchmark.![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4/figs/needleinhaystack_sabiazinho-3.png)Figure 6: Performance of the Sabiazinho-3 model in the Portuguese-adapted Needle-in-the-Haystack (NIAH) benchmark.

### 2.5 Function Calling Capabilities

The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [[17](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib17 "")] is a benchmark for evaluating the LLM’s capabilities in executing function calls and using tools effectively. The benchmark is updated periodically, and comprises three distinct subsets:

1. 1.     Non-live: An expert-curated collection of question-function-answer pairs, encompassing multiple languages and complex use cases, designed to challenge the models’ ability to understand and apply functions accurately. The examples are categorized into Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) analysis, measuring whether the function names, arguments, and parameter types match the expected response; and executable verification (Exec), which executes the function and verifies whether the output is correct.

2. 2.     Live: User-contributed examples that reflect real-world applications, ensuring that the models are tested against scenarios that mirror everyday tasks.

3. 3.     Multi turn: Multi-turn and multi-step function calling tasks that simulate agentic behaviors, requiring models to plan execution strategies, request information, and manage a sequence of function invocations to complete a task.

The benchmark also includes two categories to measure hallucinations: irrelevance detection, when none of the provided functions is relevant to the query and should not be invoked; and relevance, when at least one of the functions should be invoked.

To evaluate the models we use the original examples in English. Table [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 2.5 Function Calling Capabilities ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") shows the results of Sabiá-3, Sabiazinho-3, and other proprietary LLMs.
The results indicate that Sabiá-3 ranks competitively alongside top-performing models. It outperforms in the Non-live categories but requires enhancements in multi-turn and multi-step tasks. For instance, increasing the support for more than 32,000 tokens could improve in one of the multi-turn categories. It also needs to improve in the irrelevance category.

Table 4: Results on the BFCL benchmark ordered by overall accuracy.

### 2.6 Agentic Performance

Recent advancements in the ability of LLMs on instruction-following, function calling, and reason in long contexts have enabled the development of LLM-based agents. These agents can automatically execute complex tasks, such as developing code [[18](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib18 ""), [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib4 "")], managing everyday user tasks on operating systems [[11](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib11 ""), [12](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib12 "")], and orchestrating robots [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib3 "")].

To evaluate an LLM in agentic tasks, it is necessary to integrate it with a framework with modules for memory, action, and reasoning. This setup allows the LLM to interact with responsive environments through tools using natural language. To this end, we use AgentBench [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib10 "")], a framework designed to evaluate the agentic capabilities of LLMs across eight distinct environments. It tests the model’s performance in multi-turn open-ended generation scenarios involving coding, gaming, and web.

Here are the eight environments where the agent LLM performs tasks in AgentBench:

- •     Operating System (OS): Interacts with a real Ubuntu terminal, executing bash scripts to retrieve information about the virtual OS.

- •     Database (DB): Runs SQL queries on a database to answer high-level questions about multiple tables.

- •     Knowledge Graph (KG): Navigates a knowledge graph with 45 million entities and 3 billion facts to extract high-level insights about relationships between entities.

- •     Web Shopping (WS): Navigates an online shopping environment to make purchases from a web page.

- •     Web Browsing (WB): Browses web pages across various domains to extract information or perform high-level actions.

- •     Digital Card Game (DCG): Plays a game against a rule-based agent, analyzing cards with different abilities to defeat the opponent.

- •     Lateral Thinking Puzzle (LTP): Solves riddles by asking questions where another agent LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) can only respond with “yes”, “no”, or “irrelevant”.

- •     House-Holding (HH): Explores a virtual house, interacting with objects and performing high-level tasks.

Table [5](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#S2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 2.6 Agentic Performance ‣ 2 Evaluation ‣ Sabiá-3 Technical Report") presents the results, using the same metrics defined in the AgentBench paper [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12049v4#bib.bib10 "")]. Each environment metric ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better performance. We report the Overall Average (OA) across all environments as our primary metric. Due to the variation in mean scores across different environments, OA is the weighted average of tasks scores, normalized to a scale from 0 to 10, where the weights are inversely proportional to the average score obtained by the models evaluated in the AgentBench paper. That is, harder tasks will have a higher weight.

Table 5: Results on AgentBench.

Even though AgentBench is in English, Sabiá-3 shows competitive performance compared to models primarily trained in this language, achieving an OA of 2.9, comparable to GPT-4o Mini. Notably, Sabiá-3 shows an improvement of 2 OA over its predecessor, Sabiá-2 Medium.

Sabiá-3 particularly excels in web-grounded agentic tasks, which involve navigating through web pages to extract relevant information and perform high-level actions. It achieves the top performance in WS, with a score of 62.5, and the second-best performance in WB. However, there’s still improvement to be done in code-grounded environments such as OS and DB.

## 3 Conclusion

We introduced Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3, a family of language models focused on Brazil-related content. They improve upon our earlier Sabiá-2 models, especially in handling long texts, reasoning, and coding. Despite rivaling state-of-the-art proprietary and open-source models on knowledge-intensive tasks while having a lower per token cost, Sabiá-3 and Sabiazinho-3 still have room for improvement in multi-step tasks and following instructions accurately, both of which we plan to address in future work.

Sabi´

a-3 Technical Report

Hugo Abonizio, Thales Sales Almeida, Thiago Laitz,

Roseval Malaquias Junior, Giovana Kerche Bon´

Maritaca AI

Abstract

This report presents Sabi´

a-3, our new flagship language model, and

Sabiazinho-3, a more cost-effective sibling. The models were trained on  
a large brazilian-centric corpus. Evaluations across diverse professional  
and academic benchmarks show a strong performance on Portuguese and  
Brazil-related tasks.

Sabi´

a-3 shows large improvements in comparison

to our previous best of model, Sabia-2 Medium, especially in reasoning-  
intensive tasks. Notably, Sabi´

a-3’s average performance matches frontier

LLMs, while it is offered at a three to four times lower cost per token,  
reinforcing the benefits of domain specialization.

1

Introduction

This technical report presents the details of the development and evaluation of  
the Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 models. We trained them on a large corpus of doc-

uments written in Portuguese, with a special focus on Brazil-related resources.  
Through training, models were exposed to information relevant to Brazilian cul-  
ture, history, and context. The main objective was to have a specialized model  
that is aware of the linguistic nuances, societal norms, and regional variations  
unique to the country. Throughout this report, we show that this specialization  
allows the models to perform better in knowledge-intensive tasks.

We applied an approach of continual learning by leveraging a “generalist”

model that already acquired some level of language understanding and reasoning  
abilities, and then further trained it on our corpus of high-quality data relevant  
to the Brazilian context. The development consisted of two main phases: (1) the  
pre-training phase, in which we further train a pre-trained model on specialized  
data following a self-supervised learning strategy optimizing for the next token  
prediction objective, and (2) the post-training phase where the model is tuned  
to follow instructions and align to human preferences.

Compared to our previous release, Sabi´

a-2 [\[5\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)we have collected a signifi-

cantly larger volume of data for pre-training. In addition to the scale, we also

and model-based methods to filter out low-quality data.

Considering the challenges of training large scale models, we used TPU v5

accelerators with Jax [\[7\] ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)to perform distributed training. We combined both  
data and model parallelism to achieve high training throughput and to ensure  
efficient utilization of TPU hardware.

After pre-training, we employed a mix of human-annotated and synthetically

generated data to teach our base model to follow instructions [\[1, 2, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#12)[15, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#14)[16, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#15)[13, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#14)[8\]. ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)The instruction tuning data is composed of both human-annotated prompts  
and synthetically generated instructions targeting specific capabilities. In addi-  
tion, we also include synthetic examples to induct self-awareness abilities in the  
model [\[6\].](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)

2

Evaluation

In this section, we compare Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 with proprietary and

open-source LLMs, listed in Table [1, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#3)on various benchmarks.

2.1

Multiple-choice Exams

We have developed a benchmark suite to evaluate the Sabi´

a-3 performance on

93 academic exams, including entry-level, undergraduate, and professional cer-  
tification exams. Our focus is on multiple-choice questions from various Brazil-

For more details about the datasets, we recommend the readers to the Sabi´

2 technical report [\[5\]. ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)In addition to the 8 benchmarks introduced in [\[5\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)we  
now incorporated five new multiple-choice benchmarks:

• ENAM: The examination aims to qualify law graduates interested in par-

ticipating in magistracy selection processes promoted by federal regional  
courts, labor courts, military courts, and courts of the states and the Fed-  
eral District and territories. The benchmark covers the first edition of the  
exam, administered on April 14, 2024, and its subsequent re-application  
one month later with a different set of questions. There are 160 questions  
in total.

• CPNU: First edition of the Concurso P´ublico Nacional Unificado (Unified

National Public Competition), administered by the Ministry of Manage-  
ment and Innovation in Public Services on August 18, 2024 for filling  
permanent public positions. The benchmark includes eight exams with a  
total of 370 questions, covering the following thematic areas:

1\. Infrastructure, Exact Sciences, and Engineering;

2\. Technology, Data, and Information;

3\. Environmental, Agricultural, and Biological Sciences;

4\. Work and Public Servant Health;

5\. Education, Health, Social Development, and Human Rights;

6\. Economic Sectors and Regulation;

7\. Government Management and Public Administration; and

8\. Intermediate Level.

3

 link to page 5 link to page 6 link to page 2 

• BCB: The BCB benchmark refers to the public examination for the Cen-

tral Bank of Brazil.

This exam features objective questions with two

possible answers: true or false. It comprises three distinct exams: basic  
knowledge, information technology, and economics and finance.

• BNDES: The BNDES benchmark is the public examination for the Na-

tional Bank for Economic and Social Development. Similar to the BCB  
exam, it consists of objective questions with two alternatives: true or  
false. The benchmark includes 14 exams covering a range of subjects such  
as law, systems analysis, administration, architecture, economics, engi-  
neering, accounting, and psychology.

• CFCEQ: The CFCEQ benchmark is the technical qualification exam con-

ducted by the Federal Accounting Council (CFC). Its purpose is to assess  
the knowledge and professional competence of accountants who wish to  
work as independent auditors in organizations regulated by the CVM,  
BCB, Susep, and Previc. The benchmark comprises 12 exams.

Figure [2 ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#5)compares the performance of Sabi´

a-3, Sabi´

a-2 Medium, and GPT-

4o on the ENADE 2022 and 2023 exams. The results reveal that Sabi´

a-2 has a

higher difficulty level in engineering and economics-related areas, as indicated  
by its lowest 10 accuracies. In contrast, Sabi´

a-3 shows a significant improve-

ment in these challenging areas, achieving a 70% reduction in errors compared  
to Sabi´

a-2, particularly in Economics and Computer Engineering. Moreover,

Sabi´

a-3 demonstrates a competitive performance compared with GPT-4o, per-

forming equally well or superior in 36 of the 54 Enade exams. Despite these  
advancements, the results indicate that Sabi´

a-3 continues to face difficulties

in certain areas, notably Chemical Engineering, Mechanical Engineering, and  
Accounting, where it reached its lowest scores.

Table [2 ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#6)shows the scores of the models in 13 benchmarks derived from aca-

demic and professional exams applied after mid-2023\. The results illustrate  
that Sabi´

a-3 has a comparable level of accuracy to GPT-4o across all 93 exams

assessed. GPT-4o exhibits an advantage particularly in the Medicine bench-  
marks, while Sabi´

a-3 demonstrates a notable performance in the CPNU exams.

Furthermore, Sabi´

a-3 surpasses Llama-3.1 405B by 2 percentage points in ac-

curacy, performing equally or better in 62% of the exams. Claude 3.5 Sonnet  
achieves the highest average accuracy, although it presents a higher risk of data  
contamination due to its training data cutoff date.

In Figure [1, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#2)we show the cost per token as of October 2024 in comparison to

the average accuracy on the aforementioned exams. We have plotted a Pareto  
curve based on generalist models, i.e., the ones not specialized in the Brazilian  
context. Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 stay above this frontier, underscoring the

cost-quality benefits that result from domain specialization.

Conversation Capabilities

This section presents the benchmark we use to evaluate the Sabi´

a-3 capabilities

to engage in dialogues.

In our previous work [\[5\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)we introduced the Brazilian Chat Evaluation (BRACE-

val), a benchmark inspired on MT-Bench [\[19\] ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#16)and designed to evaluate AI assis-  
tants’ performance in following instructions, engaging in multi-turn dialogues,  
and demonstrating knowledge specific to Brazil. BRACEval consists of 150  
multi-turn questions distributed across 13 categories, including culturally rele-  
vant topics such as writing, roleplay, extraction, humanities, entity, and contra-  
diction analysis, as well as universal categories like abstention, harmful content,  
reasoning, math, and coding.

Figure [3 ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#6)compares Sabi´

a-3 with other LLMs on BRACEval. The judge is an

LLM that is given the prompt, the answer from Sabi´

a-3 and another competitor

model and decides which one won or a tie. We address position bias by calling  
the judge twice with the order of two answers swapped.

We use GPT-4-turbo (more specifically, gpt-4-1106-preview) as the judge

because, in pairwise evaluations against other models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet  
and GPT-4o, all judges — including Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4-turbo, and  
GPT-4o — consistently preferred the responses from GPT-4-turbo.

a-2 Medium, despite still

4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. A noteworthy result is GPT-4o Mini, which, despite

expensive Llama-3.1 405B in this benchmark.

2.3

Instruction-Following Capabilities

One relevant benchmark to assess LLM abilities to follow instructions is the  
IFEval [\[20\]. ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#16)IFEval consists of approximately 500 prompts including instruc-  
tions that are veriafiable programmatically such as “write in more than 400  
words”. It uses two main metrics: strict and loose. In the strict metric, the  
model’s response is checked against a set of verifiable instructions to determine  
if it followed all of them. If so, the model receives a point. If any part of the  
instruction is not followed exactly as specified, the response is deemed incorrect  
and the model does not receive a point. The loose metric is more lenient as  
it considers variations and common transformations that might occur in the  
model’s response. For example, if an instruction requires a specific phrase to be  
included at the end of an email, but the model includes that phrase with addi-  
tional text formatting like bold or italics, the loose metric might still consider

7

 link to page 8 link to page 14 link to page 8 link to page 9 link to page 9 

the instruction to be followed, whereas the strict metric would not.

Since this benchmark’s prompts and target answers are in English, we do

not expect our Portuguese-specialized model to yield significant improvements  
in this scenario. Instead, this benchmark primarily serves to assess how well  
our model can follow instructions in comparison to state-of-the-art LLMs.

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 outper-

form Sabi´

it lags behind other models evaluated in this study, including cheaper options

2.5

Function Calling Capabilities

The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [\[17\] ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#15)is a benchmark for  
evaluating the LLM’s capabilities in executing function calls and using tools  
effectively. The benchmark is updated periodically, and comprises three distinct  
subsets:

1\. Non-live: An expert-curated collection of question-function-answer pairs,

encompassing multiple languages and complex use cases, designed to chal-  
lenge the models’ ability to understand and apply functions accurately.  
The examples are categorized into Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) analysis,  
measuring whether the function names, arguments, and parameter types  
match the expected response; and executable verification (Exec), which  
executes the function and verifies whether the output is correct.

2\. Live: User-contributed examples that reflect real-world applications, en-

suring that the models are tested against scenarios that mirror everyday  
tasks.

9

 link to page 10 link to page 16 link to page 13 link to page 14 link to page 14 link to page 13 link to page 14 

3\. Multi turn: Multi-turn and multi-step function calling tasks that simulate

agentic behaviors, requiring models to plan execution strategies, request  
information, and manage a sequence of function invocations to complete  
a task.

The benchmark also includes two categories to measure hallucinations: irrel-

evance detection, when none of the provided functions is relevant to the query  
and should not be invoked; and relevance, when at least one of the functions  
should be invoked.

To evaluate the models we use the original examples in English. Table [4](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#10)

shows the results of Sabi´

a-3, Sabiazinho-3, and other proprietary LLMs. The

results indicate that Sabi´

a-3 ranks competitively alongside top-performing mod-

els. It outperforms in the Non-live categories but requires enhancements in  
multi-turn and multi-step tasks. For instance, increasing the support for more  
than 32,000 tokens could improve in one of the multi-turn categories. It also  
needs to improve in the irrelevance category.

2.6

Agentic Performance

Recent advancements in the ability of LLMs on instruction-following, function  
calling, and reason in long contexts have enabled the development of LLM-  
based agents. These agents can automatically execute complex tasks, such as  
developing code [\[18, ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#16)[4\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)managing everyday user tasks on operating systems  
[\[11, 12\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#14)and orchestrating robots [\[3\].](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#13)

To evaluate an LLM in agentic tasks, it is necessary to integrate it with a

framework with modules for memory, action, and reasoning. This setup allows  
the LLM to interact with responsive environments through tools using natu-  
ral language. To this end, we use AgentBench [\[10\], ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#14)a framework designed to  
evaluate the agentic capabilities of LLMs across eight distinct environments.  
It tests the model’s performance in multi-turn open-ended generation scenarios  
involving coding, gaming, and web.

Here are the eight environments where the agent LLM performs tasks in

AgentBench:

• Operating System (OS): Interacts with a real Ubuntu terminal, executing

bash scripts to retrieve information about the virtual OS.

• Database (DB): Runs SQL queries on a database to answer high-level

questions about multiple tables.

10

 link to page 11 link to page 14 

• Knowledge Graph (KG): Navigates a knowledge graph with 45 million

entities and 3 billion facts to extract high-level insights about relationships  
between entities.

• Web Shopping (WS): Navigates an online shopping environment to make

purchases from a web page.

• Web Browsing (WB): Browses web pages across various domains to extract

information or perform high-level actions.

• Digital Card Game (DCG): Plays a game against a rule-based agent, an-

alyzing cards with different abilities to defeat the opponent.

• Lateral Thinking Puzzle (LTP): Solves riddles by asking questions where

another agent LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) can only respond with “yes”, “no”,  
or “irrelevant”.

• House-Holding (HH): Explores a virtual house, interacting with objects

and performing high-level tasks.

Table [5 ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#11)presents the results, using the same metrics defined in the Agent-

Bench paper [\[10\]. ](1793420501323-8b2a61b8-ff23-4101-83f1-105343f5877c-file44829.html#14)Each environment metric ranges from 0 to 100, with higher  
scores indicating better performance.

We report the Overall Average (OA)

across all environments as our primary metric. Due to the variation in mean  
scores across different environments, OA is the weighted average of tasks scores,  
normalized to a scale from 0 to 10, where the weights are inversely proportional  
to the average score obtained by the models evaluated in the AgentBench paper.  
That is, harder tasks will have a higher weight.

Conclusion

We introduced Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3, a family of language models focused on

Brazil-related content. They improve upon our earlier Sabi´

a-2 models, especially

in handling long texts, reasoning, and coding. Despite rivaling state-of-the-art  
proprietary and open-source models on knowledge-intensive tasks while having a  
lower per token cost, Sabi´

a-3 and Sabiazinho-3 still have room for improvement

in multi-step tasks and following instructions accurately, both of which we plan  
to address in future work.
